title: A Practical Benchmark of Image-Restoration Networks for ASL Perfusion-Weighted Image Denoising
authors: Shaokang Wen, He Wang, Zhensen Chen, Hongwei Li
synopsis: Low signal-to-noise ratio limits the quality of arterial spin labeling perfusion-weighted images. Practical guidance on denoising model selection remains limited.
To compare convolutional and transformer networks using different input dimensionalities and prediction strategies.
Four networks were evaluated in 16 configurations using 217 training and 54 validation cases, with two conventional denoising methods included for comparison.
SwinIR and Swin U-Net showed similar numerical performance. For transformer models, 3D inputs offered small PSNR gains over three-slice inputs, whereas residual prediction markedly improved U-Net.
impact: This benchmark informs model selection for arterial spin labeling perfusion-weighted image denoising. The findings emphasize the importance of prediction strategy and suggest limited additional benefit from volumetric inputs to transformer models under the evaluated conditions.
introduction: Arterial spin labeling (ASL) perfusion-weighted images (PWI) are valuable for visual assessment of perfusion abnormalities, but their quality is limited by low signal-to-noise ratio [1]. Averaging repeated acquisitions improves image quality but increases scan time. Transformer networks have shown promise for ASL denoising [2,3], but assessing their practical value requires comparisons with established alternatives. This study compared four networks across input dimensionalities and prediction strategies to inform model selection for PWI denoising.
methods: The dataset comprised 271 cases: 67 healthy controls, 103 cases with stroke, and 101 cases with respiratory disorders; 217 were used for training and 54 for validation. All acquisitions used a gradient and spin echo (GRASE) readout. Post-labeling delays were 1500 ms in 79 cases, 1800 ms in 124 cases, and 2000 ms in 68 cases. Cases with substantial head motion were excluded, and all included data underwent motion correction. Each volume had a 64 × 64 matrix, 22–28 slices, and a nominal voxel size of approximately 3.5 × 3.5 × 6 mm³. The network input and reference target were generated by averaging 4 and 18 PWI repetitions. The 18 repetitions included the 4 used to generate the input.

U-Net [4], Pix2Pix [5], SwinIR [2,6], and a HUST-based Swin U-Net [3] were evaluated. Pseudo-3D (2.5D) models predicted the central slice from three adjacent slices; 3D models processed volumetric inputs. Networks were adapted to produce single-channel PWI outputs. Feature-channel widths and attention-window sizes were adjusted, and anisotropic operations were used in volumetric 3D models. Direct and residual prediction were evaluated for each architecture and input configuration, yielding 16 configurations. Direct prediction estimated the reference PWI. For residual prediction, the predicted residual was added to the central input slice in pseudo-3D models or to the input volume in 3D models. Three-slice input was selected based on the trade-off between noise reduction and cerebral blood flow (CBF) bias reported by Shou et al. [2]. Given their reported increase in white matter CBF bias with M0-assisted denoising, M0 was excluded from our network inputs and used only for foreground masking. BM4D and DT-CWT-NLM were included as conventional denoising methods for comparison [7,8].

Both input and reference images were normalized using min–max parameters derived from the input image, without intensity clipping. All networks used equally weighted foreground L1 and structural similarity (SSIM) losses. Pix2Pix additionally included a foreground-weighted adversarial loss with weight 0.01; its generator and discriminator used the same learning-rate decay. Networks were trained using the Adam optimizer with an initial learning rate of 0.0002 for up to 200 epochs. For each configuration, the checkpoint with the lowest mean validation reconstruction loss was selected for evaluation.

SSIM, peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), root mean squared error (RMSE), and normalized mean squared error (NMSE) were calculated independently for each case within the same foreground mask and summarized as mean ± sample standard deviation across 54 validation cases. For SSIM and PSNR, predictions and references were scaled using the input-derived min–max parameters. RMSE was calculated in original PWI intensity units; NMSE was squared error divided by reference signal energy. Visual examples were selected near the 25th and 75th percentiles of input SSIM.
results: The four-repeat input had a mean SSIM of 0.8618, PSNR of 33.40 dB, and RMSE of 8.87. BM4D and DT-CWT-NLM reduced RMSE to 8.41 and 8.18, respectively (Table 1).

The 3D residual Swin U-Net achieved the highest mean SSIM (0.9220) and PSNR (37.43 dB), and the lowest RMSE (5.44). The 3D residual SwinIR achieved the lowest NMSE (0.1052). Their SSIM, PSNR, and RMSE differed by 0.0003, 0.03 dB, and 0.02, respectively (Table 2). Across transformer configurations, PSNR was 0.05–0.23 dB higher with 3D inputs than with pseudo-3D inputs.

Residual prediction increased U-Net PSNR from 24.94 to 36.87 dB for pseudo-3D inputs and from 29.94 to 36.86 dB for 3D inputs. Pix2Pix achieved PSNR values of 35.70–35.94 dB (Tables 1 and 2). Representative denoised images and absolute error maps are shown in Figure 1.
discussion: In this cohort, SwinIR and Swin U-Net showed the best overall performance, with only minor differences between them. Three-slice pseudo-3D transformer models achieved PSNR values close to those of their volumetric counterparts, while residual U-Net remained a competitive convolutional alternative. The improvement in U-Net with residual prediction suggests that prediction strategy should be considered alongside network architecture. Although using the same validation cohort for model selection and evaluation limits assessment of generalizability, this benchmark provides a practical reference for model selection in ASL PWI denoising.
